title: Thanks due to God, not to demons
source_text: Κέλσος μὲν οὖν οἴεται τῷ βίῳ λειτουργεῖν τὰ πρέποντα. μέχρι ἂν τῶν δεσμῶν ἀπολυθῶσιν ἄνθρωποι, ἐπὰν κατὰ τὰ νενομισμένα τοῖς πολλοῖς τὰς θυσίας τις ἀποδιδῷ ἑκάστῳ τῶν κατὰ πόλιν νομιζομένων θεῶν, οὐ νοήσας τὸ ἀληθῶς πρέπον ὑπὸ τῆς ἀκριβοῦς εὐσεβείας ὑπολαμβανόμενον· ἡμεῖς δέ φαμεν τῷ βίῳ λειτουργεῖν μετὰ τῶν πρεπόντων τὸν μεμνημένον, τίς τε ὁ δημιουργήσας καὶ τίνα τὰ ἐκείνῳ φίλα, καὶ πάντα πράττοντα πρὸς τὸ φίλον τῷ θεῷ. καὶ πάλιν Κέλσος μὲν οὐ θέλει ἡμᾶς ἀχαρίστους εἶναι πρὸς τοὺς τῇδε δαίμονας, οἰόμενος ἡμᾶς ὀφείλειν αὐτοῖς χαριστήρια· καὶ ἡμεῖς δὲ τρανοῦντες τὸν περὶ εὐχαριστίας λόγον φαμὲν πρὸς τοὺς μηδὲν εὐεργετοῦντας ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ἐναντίου ἱσταμένους μηδὲν ἀχάριστον ἡμᾶς ποιεῖν, ὅταν αὐτοῖς μὴ θύωμεν ἀλλὰ μηδὲ θεραπεύωμεν αὐτούς. ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀχάριστοι εἶναι πρὸς τὸν θεὸν περιϊστάμεθα, οὗ τῶν εὐεργεσιῶν πλήρεις ἐσμὲν, καὶ δημιουργήματα ὄντες αὐτοῦ καὶ προνοούμενοι ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ κριθέντες ὅπως ποτὲ εἶναι καὶ ἔξω τοῦ βίου τὰς παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἐλπίδας ἐκδεχόμενοι. ἔστι δὲ καὶ σύμβολον ἡμῖν τῆς πρὸς θεὸν εὐχαριστίας ἄρτος „εὐχαριστία“ καλούμενος. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ δαίμονες ἔχουσιν, ὡς καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω ἐλέγομεν, τὴν οἰκονομίαν τῶν πρὸς τὰς ἡμετέρας χρείας δεδημιουργημένων· διὸ οὐδ᾿ ἄδικόν τι πράττομεν μετέχοντες τῶν δημιουργημάτων καὶ τοῖς μὴ προσήκουσιν αὐτοῖς μὴ θύοντες. κἂν ἴδωμεν δὲ μὴ δαίμονάς τινας ἀγγέλους δὲ τεταγμένους ἐπὶ τῶν τῆς γῆς καρπῶν καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς τῶν ζῴων γενέσεως, εὐφημοῦμεν αὐτοὺς καὶ μακαρίζομεν, ἐγχειρισθέντας ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ τὰ χρήσιμα τῷ γένει ἡμῶν· οὐ μὴν τὴν ὀφειλομένην πρὸς θεὸν τιμὴν τούτοις ἀπονέμομεν, οὔτε γὰρ ὁ θεὸς τοῦτο βούλεται οὔτ᾿ αὐτοὶ οἱ τὰ τοιάδε ἐγκεχειρισμένοι. καὶ ἀποδέχονταί γε ἡμᾶς φυλασσομένους αὐτοῖς θύειν ἢ θύοντας· οὐδὲ γὰρ χρῄζουσιν ἐκεῖνοι τῶν ἀπὸ γῆς ἀναθυμιωμένων.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus then thinks (οἴομαι) that [men] minister (λειτουργέω) to life the befitting things (τὰ πρέποντα), until men are released (ἀπολύω) from the bonds (δεσμός), when someone according to the customs (τὰ νενομισμένα) of the many renders (ἀποδίδωμι) the sacrifices (θυσία) to each of the gods recognised (νομίζω) city by city (κατὰ πόλιν), not having understood (νοέω) the truly fitting as conceived (ὑπολαμβάνω) by exact (ἀκριβής) piety (εὐσέβεια); but we say that he ministers to life with the befitting things who remembers (μιμνῄσκομαι) who is the one who created (δημιουργέω) and what things are dear (φίλος) to him, and does all things toward what is dear to God. And again Celsus does not wish us to be ungrateful (ἀχάριστος) toward the demons (δαίμων) here, thinking we owe (ὀφείλω) them thank-offerings (χαριστήρια); and we, making clear (τρανόω) the doctrine (λόγος) of thanksgiving (εὐχαριστία), say that toward those who benefit (εὐεργετέω) [us] nothing but rather stand (ἵσταμαι) on the opposite side we do nothing ungrateful, when we do not sacrifice (θύω) to them nor even serve (θεραπεύω) them. But we shun (περιΐσταμαι) being ungrateful toward God, of whose benefits (εὐεργεσία) we are full (πλήρης), being his creatures (δημιούργημα) and cared for (προνοέω) by him, having been judged (κρίνω) to be in whatever way (ὅπως ποτέ), and outside life awaiting (ἐκδέχομαι) the hopes (ἐλπίς) from him. And there is for us also a symbol (σύμβολον) of thanksgiving toward God, bread (ἄρτος) called 'eucharist' (εὐχαριστία). But neither do demons have, as we said above too, the management (οἰκονομία) of things created for our needs (χρεία); wherefore neither do we do anything unjust (ἄδικον) partaking (μετέχω) of the creatures and not sacrificing to those to whom they do not belong (προσήκω). And if we see (ὁράω) not demons but angels (ἄγγελος) appointed (τάσσω) over the fruits (καρπός) of the earth and over the birth (γένεσις) of animals (ζῷα), we speak well of (εὐφημέω) them and call them blessed (μακαρίζω), entrusted (ἐγχειρίζω) by God with the things useful (χρήσιμα) to our race; yet we do not assign (ἀπονέμω) to them the honour (τιμή) owed (ὀφείλω) to God, for neither does God will (βούλομαι) this nor they themselves who have been entrusted with such things. And they receive/approve (ἀποδέχομαι) us guarding against (φυλάσσομαι) sacrificing to them [rather] than sacrificing; for they do not need (χρῄζω) the things exhaled (ἀναθυμιάομαι) from earth.
pass_b_english: Celsus, then, thinks that men perform the duties that befit life, until they are released from their bonds, when they render the sacrifices, according to the customs of the many, to each of the gods recognized in each city. He has not understood what exact piety takes to be truly fitting. We, however, say that the one who performs what befits life is the one who remembers who the Creator is and what is pleasing to him, and who does all things in order to please God.

And again, Celsus does not want us to be ungrateful toward the demons here, since he thinks we owe them thank-offerings. But we, setting out clearly the teaching on thanksgiving, say that we do nothing ungrateful toward beings who do us no good but, on the contrary, stand against us, when we do not sacrifice to them, nor even serve them. What we guard against is being ungrateful toward God, whose benefits fill us. We are his creatures, cared for by him in whatever state his judgment has placed us, and beyond this life we look for the hopes that come from him. And we have a token of our thanksgiving to God: the bread called “Eucharist”, that is, “Thanksgiving”.

Nor, as we said above as well, do demons have the management of the things created for our needs. Therefore we do nothing unjust when we partake of created things and do not sacrifice to those to whom they do not belong. And if we perceive that it is not some demons but angels who are set over the fruits of the earth and the birth of living creatures, we speak well of them and call them blessed, since God has entrusted them with what is useful to our race. Yet we do not give them the honour owed to God; for neither does God wish this, nor do those entrusted with such tasks themselves. Indeed, they welcome us more when we refrain from sacrificing to them than if we sacrificed; for they have no need of the fumes that rise from the earth.

choices.choice: Origen takes up Celsus’s phrase from 8.55, τῷ βίῳ λειτουργεῖν τὰ πρέποντα, ‘perform the duties that befit life’, and gives it a Christian sense; the English keeps the phrase in both chapters. ‘Gods recognized in each city’ renders τῶν κατὰ πόλιν νομιζομένων θεῶν. τίς τε ὁ δημιουργήσας is ‘who the Creator is’ (no possessive in the Greek). ‘What is pleasing to him ... in order to please God’ renders τὰ ἐκείνῳ φίλα and πρὸς τὸ φίλον τῷ θεῷ (‘what is dear to him’); no Scripture is quoted. κριθέντες ὅπως ποτὲ εἶναι is obscure; rendered ‘in whatever state his judgment has placed us’, taking κριθέντες as God’s judgment on our condition. The bread ‘called εὐχαριστία’: the Greek word means both the sacrament and ‘thanksgiving’, which is Origen’s point; ‘that is, “Thanksgiving”’ renders that one word’s double sense and adds no idea. ‘As we said above’ refers to Origen’s earlier argument in Book 8 that the fruits of the earth belong to God, not the demons (around 8.31–34). μὴ δαίμονάς τινας ἀγγέλους δέ: τινας goes with the demons, hence ‘not some demons but angels’. ἀποδέχονταί γε ἡμᾶς φυλασσομένους ... ἢ θύοντας has comparative ἤ without μᾶλλον; rendered ‘welcome us more when we refrain ... than if we sacrificed’. κἂν ἴδωμεν rendered ‘if we perceive’ (see in the mind). The ‘fumes that rise from the earth’ are the smoke of sacrifice, which Origen elsewhere says feeds the demons; no reference is cited.
τίς τε ὁ δημιουργήσας: 'who his Creator is' ('his' added) -> 'who the Creator is'
μὴ δαίμονάς τινας ἀγγέλους δέ: 'not demons but certain angels' (τινας misplaced) -> 'not some demons but angels'
'Eucharist, that is, Thanksgiving' kept: it renders the one Greek word's double sense on which the argument turns
